problem: Recent visual-navigation foundation policies such as OmniVLA, NavFoM and NoMaD rely on a dedicated or retrained visual encoder, a bespoke continuous regression or diffusion action head, and thousands of hours of cross-embodiment data. It is unclear whether any of this is needed for short-to-medium-horizon waypoint navigation, or whether a frozen general-purpose MLLM is enough if the action representation is redesigned. Existing policies such as OmniVLA also cannot fuse an image goal with a coordinate goal and do not emit their own stop signal.
motivation: VLA benchmarking (VLM4VLA, ReVLA) points to the visual encoder as the main bottleneck, which pushes the field toward scaling perception. The authors argue instead that modern MLLM pretraining already provides broad, robust visual features. They propose that the gap to a deployable policy can be closed by aligning metric waypoints and stop decisions with the model's native token interface, using a tiny dataset. This targets structured deployments where a higher-level planner supplies local goals about 1 m-scale apart.
key_idea: LoRA-adapt only the language tower of a frozen-vision Gemma-4-E2B-it so that its stock LM head emits 8 body-frame waypoints as 64-bin value tokens, plus explicit <goal_reached>/<goal_unreachable> tokens, trained with CE plus a soft-decoded (expectation-over-bins) MSE loss on only 8.7 h of SCAND.
insight: A frozen MLLM vision tower plus a discrete action vocabulary is sufficient for real-robot waypoint navigation. Adding metric structure back to the bin distribution matters: the soft-decoded aux loss cuts ego-only val ADE from 1.05 m to 0.81 m (−23%), and continuous expectation decoding raises Warehouse ego+pose success from 3/5 to 5/5 versus argmax. The strongest lesson is that offline ADE is a poor proxy for deployability, shown in two ways: (1) a frame-aligned goal sampler has better in-distribution ADE (0.26 vs 0.49 m) but fails on the robot on every modality, always emitting <goal_reached>; its OOD pose FDE is 2.88 vs 0.19 m for the distance-based sampler. (2) Image history (h=4) improves OOD ADE from 1.45 to 1.15 m but hurts closed-loop behaviour (4/5 success, Δ 0.86 m); unmatched-window tests attribute this to a time-lagged 'continue previous motion' effect of past frames. Other negative findings: raising LoRA rank to 64 at fixed α is worse, and adding in-domain TokenWalker data hurt image-goal behaviour (4/10→1/10), likely by inducing a forward-march prior.
method: Frozen-vision MLLM backbone: Gemma-4-E2B-it with the vision tower fully frozen and no auxiliary encoder; LoRA (r=32, α=16, dropout 0) on q/k/v/o/gate/up/down projections of the language tower only; predictions go through the stock LM head with no extra heads.

Value-bin trajectory tokenization: 69 reserved <unusedN> tokens are repurposed as 64 uniform bins per axis over [−15, 15] m (0.469 m per bin) plus role tokens <bot_traj>, <eot_traj>, <goal_reached>, <goal_coord>, <goal_unreachable>. Output is an 18-token sequence (8 (x,y) waypoints in the body frame), or a 3-token stop sequence. The 2D goal coordinate is fed in with the same bin tokens after <goal_coord>.

Soft-decoded auxiliary loss: logits are restricted to the 64 bin tokens and softmaxed; the expectation over bin centres gives a continuous prediction. An MSE term on this prediction (λ_aux=0.1, trajectory samples only) is added to token cross-entropy, restoring ordinal/metric structure.
Continuous decoding at inference: waypoints are the softmax expectation over bin centres (sub-bin precision) rather than the greedy argmax bin.

Data pipeline: a distance-based goal sampler draws arc-length d~U(0.5, 14) m instead of a fixed frame offset. About 10% of image-goal samples swap in a goal image from another trajectory and are labelled <goal_unreachable>. Other steps: left-right flip augmentation, a behind-robot filter (x_g < −0.3 m), and a rotation-in-place filter (>30° yaw) on stop samples. Goal modalities are ego (image), pose (coordinate), and ego+pose.

Four-phase warm-start LoRA chain (A fresh → B warm-start → C1 specialise on ego+pose → C2 broaden to all modalities): 40k steps per phase, AdamW with lr 1e-4, bf16, batch 1 per device. Input images are 224×224 (≤256 visual tokens each), with optional h∈{2,4} history frames.

Deployment on Boston Dynamics Spot: RealSense RGB at 2 Hz with a 'stretch' resize, goal pose from LiDAR-inertial SLAM (Wildcat). Inference uses torch.compile with a static KV cache and cached goal-image features, taking 1768→421 ms on A100 and 1479→1129 ms on Jetson Thor per call.

numbers_note:
No canonical embodied-navigation benchmark is used. All results are offline ADE/FDE on SCAND/TokenWalker 500-sample subsets or real Spot trials (n=4–6 per cell), with SR printed as stop/partial/miss tallies, encoded here as separate counts. Several internal inconsistencies across manifests and tables should be kept in mind:
- The deployed model's TW combined ADE is 1.19 in Table 1 (rebuilt manifest) but 1.45 in the history and goal-sampling ablation tables (earlier lagged-position manifest).
- Table 1 gives in-dist pose ADE 0.37 and ego+pose 0.33 for the deployed continuous-decode checkpoint. The decode-mode table assigns 0.37/0.33 to bin-snapped and 0.32/0.28 to continuous.
- Chemical Yard ego+pose trials are described but no numbers are tabulated.
results: GemNav reaches the goal with an autonomous stop in all 20 pose-goal trials across four unseen real environments (5/0/0 each), with final displacement 0.25–0.42 m. The OmniVLA released checkpoint fails every pose trial (0/0/5, or 0/0/4 in Warehouse), with final displacement 3.10–29.18 m. On the two long courses GemNav comes close to a human teleoperator in time and path length (e.g. Warehouse 37.9 s / 32.14 m vs human 34.2 s / 31.83 m). Offline, it scores combined ADE 0.49 m on SCAND and 1.19 m on OOD TokenWalker. Image-only goals remain weak (1/5 stops in Carpark vs OmniVLA 0/5).
limitations: Trained on a single 8.7 h corpus and deployed on a single robot (Spot); cross-embodiment transfer is untested. Evaluation uses small n (4–6 trials per cell) on custom real-world courses, not standard benchmarks.

Autonomous stopping with a pure image goal is unreliable, so the policy depends on a goal coordinate from SLAM. The 2D (x,y) output cannot express in-place rotation and filters out goals behind the robot.

A time-lagged trajectory effect can cause overshoot, and past-frame history hurts closed-loop control. Inference is slow for onboard use (~421 ms on A100 after optimization, 1129 ms on Jetson Thor, 6.5 s on Orin).
